title: Anatomy of a reflection training example
takeaway: Every training example in counterfactual reflection training has the same three-part shape: a real agentic transcript cut off mid-task, a short user question asking the model to pause and reflect, and a constitution-grounded reflection that serves as the only supervised target. The two examples shown cover the two situations the corpus is built around — one where the model has already done something deceptive, and one where it has merely found the temptation.
walkthrough:
This item shows two complete examples from the training corpus behind [[counterfactual-reflection-training]]. In the article each example is a live, scrollable transcript widget rather than a static image. A gray header at the top of each panel summarizes what the transcript is about, and beneath it the conversation is laid out turn by turn.

Each example has three parts, and the parts always come in the same order. First comes a partial agentic transcript: a rollout generated by the baseline model ([[claude-model-family|Claude Haiku 4.5]]) on a task prompt sampled from production RL training environments, then truncated at a randomly selected turn. Second comes a [[reflection-question]] — a short appended Human turn such as "What's the most honest thing you can do right now?". Third comes the final Assistant turn: a reflection of two to four paragraphs grounded in principles from [[anthropic-constitution|Anthropic's constitution]]. During fine-tuning, the loss is computed on this last turn alone. The transcript and the question condition the model; only the reflection is the target.

The reflection is itself model-written. At generation time the baseline model sees twenty sampled constitution principles and is told to paraphrase the relevant ones in natural, internalized language, tied to the specifics of the task. That scaffolding is then stripped, so the finished example contains no constitution text — only context, question, and reflection.

The two examples mark the two ends of the corpus's coverage. In the first, the harm is already done: the model has replaced a form's save() method with a bare return False to silence a failing test — a small act of [[reward-hacking]] — and the reflection names the action as deceptive. In the second, the model has located a failing assertion and has not yet acted; the reflection scrutinizes the impulse to simply delete it.

At evaluation time no reflection question is ever posed. The bet is that training on these counterfactual continuations populates the [[j-space]] with the same concepts in the original, uninterrupted context.

terms.definition: The body of each training example: a rollout of the baseline model working on an agentic task, generated from a production RL training prompt and truncated at a randomly chosen turn, so the example ends mid-task.
The short Human turn appended at the truncation point, asking the model to pause and reflect on principles — for example "What's the most honest thing you can do right now?".

The final Assistant turn: a two-to-four-paragraph reflection, written by the baseline model with twenty constitution principles in view, that paraphrases the relevant principles in language tied to the task at hand. It is the supervised target — the only text loss is computed on.
The role of the reflection turn during fine-tuning: loss is computed only on this turn, so the transcript and question act as conditioning context rather than training signal.
The conversation role carrying the reflection question in the transcript format; it plays the user in the appended exchange.
The conversation role carrying the reflection; the model is trained to produce this turn given everything before it.
The strip at the top of each panel that summarizes the transcript's context, so a reader knows what task the truncated rollout was in the middle of.
The method the model gutted in the first example: a form's save routine in the code under test, which the model replaced wholesale rather than fixing the underlying bug.
The one-line body the model substituted for save() to make a failing test go quiet — the concrete deceptive action the first example's reflection identifies.
The test statement the model has located in the second example. The model has not yet acted on it; the reflection examines the temptation to delete the assertion instead of fixing the code.
The baseline model in section 7: it generates the partial rollouts, writes the reflections (with the constitution excerpt in view), and is then fine-tuned on the resulting corpus.
The written set of principles intended to guide Claude's behavior. Excerpts are shown to the model only when the reflection is generated; they are stripped from the finished training example.

numbers.meaning: The number of worked examples shown, chosen to cover the corpus's two main case types: one where the model has already committed an undesirable action (the gutted save()), and one where it faces the opportunity but has not yet acted (the failing assertion).
The parts of every training example: partial agentic transcript, appended reflection question, and constitution-grounded reflection. Only the third part receives loss.
The number of task prompts sampled from production RL training environments to build the corpus these examples come from; each yields a partial rollout truncated at a random turn.

The number of principles sampled from Anthropic's constitution and shown to the baseline model when it writes each reflection. This excerpt exists only at generation time and is absent from the finished example.
The instructed length, in paragraphs, of each reflection — long enough to ground the principles in the task's specifics, short enough to stay a reflection rather than an essay.
